definition: Berate means to scold loudly and at length.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word berate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know berate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The bus driver berated the fare-jumper all the way to the next stop, and the whole bus rode in silence.
Nagging pesters in small, repeated doses — it never rises to berate's sustained roar.
A scolding is sharp but brief; it stops short of berate, which is loud and keeps going.

To excoriate is to flay someone with savage criticism, and it is most at home in print — reviews, reports, and editorials excoriate. Berate is spoken and face-to-face, and volume and duration are its signature: the listener stands there while it rolls over them. Critics excoriate; furious coaches berate.

A rebuke is sharp disapproval delivered sternly and briefly — one cutting sentence can be a rebuke, and then it is over. Berate runs the other way: loud, sustained, a scolding that fills the room and keeps going. A rebuke is a slap of words; berating is a storm of them.

Berate keeps an extinct English verb alive: rate once meant 'to scold angrily' all by itself. That rate died out around Shakespeare's time, leaving berate no living relatives — the rate on a menu or a report card comes from Latin ratus and is no kin at all.
Berate means to scold loudly and at length.
When the caterer arrived an hour late, the bride's father berated him in the hotel lobby until the manager steered them both into an office.
Berate means to scold loudly and at length — both parts matter.
A chide is a sentence and a scolding is a minute, but a berating fills the room and keeps going; the listener stands there while it rolls over them.
Berate is the loud, sustained, face-to-face scolding — pick it when volume and duration are the point.
Its unit-mates scale neatly: chide (gentle), admonish (firm, measured), chastise (severe, official), berate (loud and long).
A tirade, meanwhile, is the speech itself, not the act of aiming it at someone.

berate: A scolding is sharp but brief; it stops short of berate, which is loud and keeps going.
The first time I crossed on the island ferry, the bosun berated a deckhand for a sloppy coil of rope, and the scolding lasted from the harbor mouth to the first channel marker.
Passengers studied their shoes.
The deckhand stood at attention, soaked, while the words kept coming, loud enough to carry over the engines.
An older crewman told me later that nobody remembered the bosun ever writing a man up.
'Paper is quiet,' he said.
'She is not.' The strange thing was what followed: the same deckhand, an hour on, laughing with her at the wheelhouse door as if nothing had happened.
On that boat, a dressing-down was weather — loud, long, and then gone — and you were expected to sail on through it.
